theory.title: Understanding an Analog Clock
theory.theory: An analog clock has 12 numbered positions and 60 minute divisions around a full 360° circle. The minute hand completes one revolution in 60 minutes, the hour hand completes one revolution in 12 hours, and the second hand completes one revolution in 60 seconds. Because the hour hand moves continuously, its position between two numbers depends on the minutes elapsed after the hour.
formulas: Hour hand = 0.5° per minute = 1/120° per second
shortcuts: Memorize 6° per minute for the minute hand.
Memorize 30° per hour for the hour hand.
Add 0.5° for every minute after the hour to the hour hand position.

examples.question: Where is the minute hand at 20 minutes?

commonMistakes: Treating the hour hand as fixed at its number.
Confusing minutes with hour divisions.
examTips: Draw a quick clock if the wording is difficult.
Keep the hour hand's fractional movement.

theory.title: Main Clock Angle Formula
theory.theory: At H:M, the minute hand is M×6 degrees from 12. The hour hand is H×30 + M×0.5 degrees from 12. Their raw separation is |30H−5.5M|. Since two angles are formed around a circle, the smaller angle is the minimum of this value and 360° minus this value.
shortcuts: For an exact integer minute, substitute directly into |30H−5.5M|.
If the raw difference exceeds 180°, subtract it from 360°.

examples.question: Find the angle at 4:20.

commonMistakes: Using 30H−6M, which ignores hour-hand movement.
Reporting the larger angle when the question asks for the smaller angle.
examTips: Always calculate the hour hand using 30H+0.5M.

theory.title: Finding a Time for a Given Angle
theory.theory: To find when an angle θ occurs during a specified hour, solve |30H−5.5M|=θ. The absolute value creates two equations: 30H−5.5M=θ and 30H−5.5M=−θ. Test both solutions and keep only minutes from 0 through less than 60.
shortcuts: Solve both signs; an hour can contain two occurrences of many angles.
Convert decimal minutes into seconds when exact precision is required.

examples.question: When are the hands 90° apart between 3 and 4?
examples.solution: Set |90−5.5M|=90. One solution is M=0; the other is M=180/5.5=32 8/11 minutes.

commonMistakes: Keeping a solution where M≥60.
Assuming every specified angle occurs twice in every one-hour interval.
examTips: Check the interval stated in the question.

theory.title: When Hands Overlap
theory.theory: Coincidence means the hour and minute hands occupy the same position. The minute hand moves at 6°/minute and the hour hand at 0.5°/minute, so the minute hand gains 5.5°/minute. It needs 360° of relative movement to catch the hour hand again.
shortcuts: Coincidence after H:00 occurs at M=60H/11 minutes for H=0,1,...,11.

examples.question: When do the hands coincide between 3 and 4?

commonMistakes: Saying 12 coincidences in 12 hours; the standard count is 11 occurrences.
Using 60 minutes as the interval.
examTips: Remember 720/11 minutes as the coincidence interval.

theory.title: 180° Separation
theory.theory: Opposite hands are 180° apart. Set |30H−5.5M|=180. The relative motion still has speed 5.5°/minute. There are 11 opposite positions in a 12-hour cycle.
shortcuts: Solve the same way as specified-angle problems, using θ=180°.

examples.question: Find the first opposite position after 8:00.
examples.solution: |240−5.5M|=180. The valid first solution is M=60/5.5=10 10/11 minutes.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the hour hand has moved.
Counting the 180° position as a coincidence.
examTips: Treat 180° as a special specified-angle problem.

theory.title: 90° Separation
theory.theory: A right angle occurs when the hands are separated by 90°. Solve |30H−5.5M|=90. There are 22 right-angle occurrences in 12 hours and 44 in 24 hours.
shortcuts: Use the specified-angle equation with θ=90.

examples.question: When are the hands 90° apart after 1:00?
examples.solution: |30−5.5M|=90. The valid solution is M=120/5.5=21 9/11 minutes.

commonMistakes: Assuming the right angle always occurs at :15 or :45.
examTips: The hour hand moves, so exact quarter-hour shortcuts are usually wrong.

theory.title: Fast and Slow Clocks
theory.theory: A fast clock gains time relative to real time; a slow clock loses time. If a clock gains g minutes every hour, its shown elapsed time for each real hour is 60+g minutes. If it loses l minutes every hour, it shows 60−l minutes per real hour. For a stated synchronization point, use a ratio between displayed elapsed time and actual elapsed time.
shortcuts: Convert all rates to the same unit before solving.
A gain/loss question needs a reference or synchronization time to determine an absolute displayed reading.

examples.question: A clock gains 5 min per hour. Gain in 12 hours?

commonMistakes: Assuming a clock's current displayed time alone reveals the actual time without a starting condition.
examTips: Write a timeline when the question gives a starting synchronization.

theory.title: Reading a Mirror Image
theory.theory: For a standard 12-hour analog clock, the mirror reverses the positions around the vertical axis. The shortcut is mirror time = 11:60 − actual time. For example, 7:25 gives 4:35.
formulas: Actual time from mirror = 11:60 − mirror reading
shortcuts: For exact 12:00, the mirror also reads 12:00.

examples.question: Mirror image of 10:10?

commonMistakes: Using 12:00−time without converting the borrowing correctly.
examTips: Write 11:60 before subtracting.

theory.title: Mixed and Expert Clock Reasoning
theory.theory: Advanced clock questions combine relative motion, specified angles, multiple occurrences, mirror readings, and fast/slow rates. The safest approach is to define the unknown minute or elapsed time, write the governing equation, solve both absolute-value branches when needed, and check the result against the stated interval.
formulas: Fast/slow: displayed rate relative to actual rate
shortcuts: Break a mixed problem into independent conditions.
Check units: degrees, minutes, hours and seconds must not be mixed.

examples.question: A clock question combines a specified angle and a time interval. What is the first step?
examples.solution: Translate the hand positions into degrees and write the absolute-value angle equation before solving.

commonMistakes: Solving an equation without checking whether the time lies in the requested hour.
examTips: Verification is part of the solution, not an optional step.

formulas: Coincidence count = 11 in 12 hours; 22 in 24 hours
Right-angle count = 22 in 12 hours; 44 in 24 hours
Fast clock: displayed rate = 60+gain minutes per real hour
Slow clock: displayed rate = 60−loss minutes per real hour
shortcuts: 6° per minute for minute hand
30° per hour and 0.5° per minute for hour hand
5.5° per minute relative movement
720/11-minute coincidence interval
Solve specified angles with ±θ
Mirror: 11:60 − actual
Use rate ratios for fast/slow clocks
Do not use shortcuts without checking the stated interval

theory.title: Calendar Fundamentals
theory.theory: The Gregorian calendar divides time into weeks of 7 days and years of 365 days, with 366 days in a leap year. Months have 28, 29, 30 or 31 days. Weekday questions can be solved by counting total days and reducing modulo 7.
shortcuts: Remember the 30/31-day month pattern and February exception.

examples.question: How many days are in a normal year?

commonMistakes: Forgetting February has 29 days in leap years.
examTips: Decide first whether the relevant year is leap or common.

theory.title: Gregorian Leap-Year Rule
theory.theory: A Gregorian year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except century years. A century year is a leap year only if it is divisible by 400. Therefore 1900 and 2100 are not leap years, while 2000 and 2400 are leap years.
formulas: Divisible by 100 → not leap unless divisible by 400
shortcuts: Check 400 first for century years.

examples.question: Is 2000 leap?

commonMistakes: Calling every year divisible by 4 a leap year.
examTips: Century rule is a frequent exam trap.

theory.title: Odd Days Method
theory.theory: Odd days are the remainder after dividing a total number of days by 7. A normal year has 365 = 52 weeks + 1 day, so it contributes 1 odd day. A leap year contributes 2 odd days. Add odd days across the required years and reduce modulo 7.
shortcuts: For long ranges, count leap years separately.
A 400-year Gregorian cycle contributes 0 odd days.

examples.question: Odd days in a leap year?

commonMistakes: Treating 100 years as a fixed odd-day count without specifying the century interval.
examTips: State the exact start and end years for century calculations.

theory.title: Days in Each Month
theory.theory: January, March, May, July, August, October and December have 31 days. April, June, September and November have 30. February has 28 in a common year and 29 in a leap year.
formulas: 31-day months: Jan, Mar, May, Jul, Aug, Oct, Dec
shortcuts: Use the knuckle method or the mnemonic: Thirty days hath September, April, June and November.

examples.question: Days in September?

commonMistakes: Treating July and August as having different lengths.
examTips: In date differences, write a month table if needed.

theory.title: Finding a Weekday
theory.theory: To find a weekday, choose a known reference date or use an odd-days method. Compute the number of elapsed days, divide by 7, and shift the reference weekday by the remainder. Gregorian rules must be applied when the range crosses leap years or centuries.
formulas: New weekday = reference weekday + (elapsed days mod 7)
shortcuts: Only the remainder modulo 7 affects the weekday.

examples.question: If Monday is today, what day is it after 100 days?

commonMistakes: Using the quotient instead of the remainder.
examTips: Keep weekday indexing consistent.

theory.title: Before and After N Days
theory.theory: A shift of N days changes the weekday by N mod 7. For an actual date, add or subtract a timedelta-style number of calendar days, allowing month lengths and leap days to change the date.
shortcuts: Reduce large N modulo 7 for weekday-only questions.

examples.question: Sunday minus 75 days?

commonMistakes: Reversing before and after.
examTips: Draw a seven-day cycle for negative shifts.

theory.title: Counting Days Between Dates
theory.theory: Date-difference questions require careful counting across month and year boundaries. For elapsed days, subtract the earlier date from the later date; the starting date is not counted as a completed day. Leap days must be included when they occur within the interval.
formulas: Elapsed days = later date − earlier date
Inclusive count = elapsed days + 1 when both endpoints are counted
shortcuts: For 1 January to 1 January, the difference is the number of days in the intervening years.

examples.question: 1 Jan 2020 to 1 Jan 2025?

commonMistakes: Confusing elapsed and inclusive counting.
examTips: Read whether the question says 'between', 'from...to', or 'including both dates'.

theory.title: 100, 200, 300 and 400 Year Cycles
theory.theory: Century calculations depend on which century is being used because century years can be non-leap. In the Gregorian calendar, every 400-year block contains 97 leap years and 303 common years, totaling 146097 days, exactly divisible by 7.
shortcuts: Group large ranges into complete 400-year blocks.

examples.question: Odd days in 400 years?

commonMistakes: Assuming every century contains 25 leap years.
examTips: Check century years individually unless you can group a complete 400-year cycle.

theory.title: Finding a Repeating Calendar
theory.theory: Two years have the same calendar when they have the same weekday for 1 January and the same leap/common status, so every month aligns. The accumulated weekday shift from intervening years determines the candidate; then verify the year types.
formulas: Same calendar requires same 1 January weekday + same leap/common status
shortcuts: Do not stop after matching 1 January; check leap status.

examples.question: Next same calendar after 2025?
examples.solution: 2031 has the same 1 January weekday and is also a common year.

commonMistakes: Matching only January 1.
examTips: Always perform the two-condition check.

theory.title: Calendar Cycles
theory.theory: A common-year weekday pattern shifts by one day in the next year; a leap-year pattern shifts by two. The familiar 28-year cycle is a useful shortcut in many ranges, but century exceptions interrupt simple 28-year repetition. The exact Gregorian cycle is 400 years.
shortcuts: Use 28-year patterns only when no century exception breaks the sequence.

examples.question: Why does a 400-year cycle repeat?

commonMistakes: Using a 28-year repeat blindly across 2100, 2200 or 2300.
examTips: Use the 400-year rule for long Gregorian ranges.

theory.title: Birthday Weekday Problems
theory.theory: Birthday questions combine date intervals with weekday shifts. For an ordinary birthday, count the intervening days and include leap days when they occur before the birthday in the relevant year. Leap-day birthdays require an explicit convention if the question asks about non-leap years.
formulas: Leap day contributes one additional shift when crossed
shortcuts: Compare the same month/day first; then count year shifts.

examples.question: If 1 January 2024 is Monday, what day is 1 January 2025?
examples.solution: 2024 is leap, so shift by 2 days: Monday→Wednesday.

commonMistakes: Treating every year as a 1-day shift.
examTips: Identify leap years between the two birthdays.

theory.title: Mixed Calendar Reasoning
theory.theory: Expert problems may combine large date ranges, century rules, same-calendar conditions, date differences and modular arithmetic. Solve them by splitting the interval into manageable year blocks, applying the exact leap-year rule, and reducing the final total modulo 7.
shortcuts: Peel off complete 400-year cycles first.
Use exact date arithmetic near February and century boundaries.

examples.question: How many days from 1 January 2000 to 1 January 2400?

commonMistakes: Ignoring the endpoint convention or century exception.
examTips: Write the interval endpoints explicitly before counting.

formulas: Leap year: divisible by 4, except century years unless divisible by 400
Elapsed date difference = later date − earlier date
Same calendar requires same 1 January weekday and same leap/common status
shortcuts: N mod 7 for weekday shifts
Normal year contributes 1 odd day
Leap year contributes 2 odd days
Check century years with divisibility by 400
Group complete 400-year cycles
Use month-length table
Do not confuse elapsed with inclusive date counts
Verify same-calendar candidates using both conditions
